raw_response:
I farm only 6 mu, and at my age I do not want to take big risks. We have done wheat-maize for many years, and that is still the safest way for my family. Wheat gives a steady harvest, and maize follows right after, so even if one side is not perfect, I still have income from the land. I finished middle school, so I do listen to what the township technicians say, but in the end I still go by what worked on my own fields and what nearby farmers are doing.

For wheat, I will keep the full 6 mu in winter wheat. In Quzhou the usual time is early October, and I do not want to sow too late because late wheat does not tiller well. I will use a common improved variety from the local dealer, not the most expensive seed. On fertilizer, I usually do a base application first, then one topdressing around jointing. If I cut too much fertilizer, I worry the leaves will go yellow and the ears will be small, so I would rather stay a little heavier than too light, but I still have to watch cash. I have well water, so I plan around 3 irrigations for wheat if rainfall is normal: one after sowing if the soil is dry, one at overwintering or reviving stage depending on moisture, and one around jointing. If spring is dry, I may add one more, but pumping costs money, so I will not irrigate just for peace of mind.

After wheat harvest, I will plant summer maize on the same 6 mu right away. The turnaround is tight, so I will keep tillage simple and use quick field prep. I do not have spare labor at home, and some family labor is away working, so I cannot afford a slow method. I will use hybrid maize seed because the local hybrids usually yield better and emerge more evenly. For maize I will apply some fertilizer at planting and then one topdress when it is knee-high to waist-high. If rain is decent, maybe I only irrigate once or even not at all, but if it is dry during tasseling, I will use the well because that stage affects grain badly. I do not spray unless I see a real problem, especially for insects or heavy weeds, because every bottle costs money. I am not chasing the highest yield. I want a stable crop, manageable labor, and enough cash left in hand in case something unexpected happens.
